title: Personal Details of 40,000 Homeland Security Workers Appear Online
summary: A website that shares leaked documents said on Wednesday that it had published personal details of more than 40,000 people who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, known as DHS, which handles border security and disaster response. The shared data includes names, phone numbers, email addresses, and job titles from DHS agencies. Some job titles revealed sensitive assignments in special operations, surveillance, computer forensics, and undercover work. Distributed Denial of Secrets, the group behind the release, said the information came from an entity calling itself the Department of Peace, and that the data was harvested from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Okta said it is secure and has no evidence its data or systems were compromised. DHS said it was aware of a breach and was working to address it and protect its employees. Reuters said it could not verify the entire trove, but it matched details about six employees to credit bureau records and confirmed three employees' phone numbers by calling them. This is the third government data leak in the past month.
why_it_matters: Keeping passwords and personal details private matters because sharing them online can put people at risk, just like keeping your own login details secret at school.

keywords.explanation: Surveillance means watching people or places closely, often to gather information.
Computer forensics is the work of finding clues in computers and digital files.
Undercover work is secret work done while hiding who you really are.
A breach is when private information is taken or shared without permission.
If a system is compromised, someone has broken into it or weakened its safety.
